chunks.heading: What is matter?
chunks.body: Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space. Almost everything around you, from air to rock, counts as matter.
chunks.checkText: Which best describes matter?

checkOptions.text: Anything with mass that takes up space
Only solid objects you can hold

chunks.heading: Elements: one type of atom
chunks.body: An element is a kind of [[chem-matter-basics|matter]] made of only one type of atom. Elements can't be broken down into anything simpler.
chunks.checkText: Can an element be broken down into simpler substances?

checkOptions.text: No, elements are already the simplest substances
Yes, by dissolving them in water

chunks.heading: Noble gases: solo atoms
chunks.body: Some [[chem-element-basics|elements]] exist as single, separate atoms rather than joining together. These are called monatomic elements, and include the noble gases like helium and neon.
chunks.checkText: Monatomic elements exist as...

chunks.heading: Elements that form molecules
chunks.body: Many non-metal [[chem-element-basics|elements]] bond into small groups called molecules. For example, sulfur atoms bond together in groups of eight to form a single sulfur molecule.
chunks.checkText: A molecule made only of sulfur atoms is an example of...

chunks.heading: Elements that form giant networks
chunks.body: Some non-metal elements bond into a giant 3D network instead of small [[chem-element-molecules|molecules]]. Carbon does this, forming diamond or graphite.
chunks.checkText: Diamond is an example of a non-metal element forming...

chunks.heading: Compounds: atoms chemically joined
chunks.body: A compound is made of two or more different [[chem-element-basics|elements]] chemically bonded together in a fixed ratio. Water is a compound of hydrogen and oxygen.
chunks.checkText: In a compound, the different elements are...

checkOptions.text: Chemically bonded together in a fixed ratio

chunks.heading: Compound or mixture?
chunks.body: A [[chem-compound-basics|compound]]'s elements are chemically bonded, so separating them usually needs a chemical reaction. A mixture's parts are only physically combined, so they're much easier to separate.
chunks.checkText: Which is generally easier to separate back into its parts?

chunks.heading: Homogeneous mixtures
chunks.body: A homogeneous mixture is the same all the way through. Every sample you take from it looks and behaves the same, like salt fully stirred into water.
chunks.checkText: In a homogeneous mixture, every sample you take...

checkOptions.text: Looks the same as any other sample
Looks different depending on where it's taken from

chunks.heading: Heterogeneous mixtures
chunks.body: Unlike a [[chem-homogeneous-mixture|homogeneous mixture]], a heterogeneous mixture is uneven. Different parts of it can look different, like pebbles mixed into sand, where the heavier pebbles sink to the bottom.
chunks.checkText: A heterogeneous mixture is one where...

checkOptions.text: Different samples of it can look different
Every sample looks exactly the same

chunks.heading: Solutions: solute in solvent
chunks.body: A solution is a [[chem-homogeneous-mixture|homogeneous]] mixture where a solute dissolves completely into a solvent. The solvent is whichever substance is present in the greater amount.
chunks.checkText: In a solution, the solute...

checkOptions.text: Is fully dissolved into the solvent
Settles at the bottom over time
Is always the substance in the greater amount

chunks.heading: Aqueous solutions: water as solvent
chunks.body: An aqueous [[chem-solution-basics|solution]] is simply one where water is the solvent. Salt dissolved in water is a common example.
chunks.checkText: An aqueous solution always has which solvent?

chunks.heading: Suspensions: mixtures that settle
chunks.body: A suspension is a [[chem-heterogeneous-mixture|heterogeneous]] mixture where the solid doesn't fully dissolve. Over time, the solid particles settle out, or they can be separated by filtering.
chunks.checkText: In a suspension, the solid particles...

checkOptions.text: Don't fully dissolve, and can settle out

chunks.heading: Colloids: in between mixtures
chunks.body: A colloid has tiny particles spread evenly through a liquid, but unlike a [[chem-suspension|suspension]], they never settle out or separate. Milk is a colloid of fat spread through water.
chunks.checkText: Unlike the particles in a suspension, the particles in a colloid...

checkOptions.text: Stay spread out and don't settle
Sink to the bottom over time
Form a separate layer on top

chunks.heading: Physical changes
chunks.body: A physical change alters how [[chem-matter-basics|matter]] looks or feels, but not what it's made of. Crushing, bending or melting something are all physical changes.
chunks.checkText: A physical change is one where...

checkOptions.text: The substance stays the same, just its form changes
A brand new substance is created

chunks.heading: Three states of matter
chunks.body: [[chem-matter-basics|Matter]] is usually found in one of three states: solid, liquid or gas.
chunks.checkText: The three most common states of matter are...

chunks.heading: The particle model
chunks.body: The particle model pictures matter as tiny particles that are always moving and attracted to each other. How strong that attraction is explains why solids, liquids and gases behave so differently.
chunks.checkText: According to the particle model, particles are...

checkOptions.text: Always moving and attracted to each other

chunks.heading: Particles in a solid
chunks.body: In a solid, [[chem-particle-model|particles]] are packed tightly and held in fixed positions by strong attraction. They can only vibrate, not move past each other.
chunks.checkText: In a solid, the particles...

chunks.heading: Particles in a liquid
chunks.body: Unlike in a [[chem-solid-particles|solid]], liquid particles are held together more loosely, so they can slide past each other. This lets a liquid flow and take the shape of its container.
chunks.checkText: A liquid can flow because its particles...

checkOptions.text: Have no attraction between them at all

chunks.heading: Particles in a gas
chunks.body: Unlike in a [[chem-liquid-particles|liquid]], the attraction between gas particles is very weak, so they spread far apart and move freely in every direction. This is why a gas fills any container it's put in.
chunks.checkText: Gas particles spread far apart because...

checkOptions.text: The attraction between them is very weak
The attraction between them is very strong

chunks.heading: Heating speeds particles up
chunks.body: Adding heat makes [[chem-particle-model|particles]] move faster and spread further apart. Enough heat can overcome the attraction holding a solid or liquid together, causing it to change state.
chunks.checkText: Heating a substance makes its particles...

checkOptions.text: Move faster and spread further apart
Move slower and pack closer together

chunks.heading: Melting and freezing
chunks.body: When [[chem-heating-particles|heating]] gives particles enough energy, a solid melts into a liquid. Cooling reverses this: freezing turns a liquid back into a solid.
chunks.checkText: Freezing is the change from...

chunks.heading: Boiling and condensing
chunks.body: Boiling is a liquid turning into a gas when heated. Condensing is the reverse: a gas turning back into a liquid when cooled.
chunks.checkText: Condensing is the change from...

chunks.heading: Sublimation: skipping the liquid
chunks.body: Unlike [[chem-melting-freezing|melting]], sublimation is when a solid turns directly into a gas without ever becoming a liquid. Dry ice, solid carbon dioxide, does this.
chunks.checkText: Sublimation is a change directly from...

chunks.heading: Separating mixtures by physical properties
chunks.body: Because a [[chem-compound-vs-mixture|mixture]]'s parts are only physically combined, they can be separated using their different physical properties, like particle size or boiling point.
chunks.checkText: Mixtures can be separated because their parts...

chunks.heading: Filtration
chunks.body: Filtration uses a filter to trap solid particles while letting liquid pass through. The liquid that passes through is called the filtrate.
chunks.checkText: During filtration, the liquid that passes through the filter is called the...

chunks.heading: Evaporation
chunks.body: Evaporation separates a dissolved solid from a liquid by letting the liquid turn to vapour and escape, leaving the solid behind.
chunks.checkText: Evaporation works by removing the...

checkOptions.text: Liquid, as it turns to vapour
Solid, as it turns to vapour

chunks.heading: Crystallisation
chunks.body: Crystallisation happens when a dissolved solid comes out of solution and forms crystals, often as the solvent [[chem-evaporation|evaporates]]. The solid that forms is called a precipitate.
chunks.checkText: A solid that forms and separates out of a solution is called a...

chunks.heading: Distillation
chunks.body: Unlike simple [[chem-evaporation|evaporation]], distillation separates a mixture of liquids using their different boiling points. The more volatile liquid boils off first, then is cooled back into a liquid and collected.
chunks.checkText: Distillation separates a mixture of liquids based on their different...

chunks.heading: Percentage composition
chunks.body: Percentage composition tells you what percentage of a [[chem-compound-basics|compound]]'s mass comes from each element. It's found using: mass of element ÷ mass of compound x 100.
chunks.checkText: Percentage composition by mass tells you...

checkOptions.text: What percentage of the total mass each element contributes
How many atoms of each element there are

chunks.heading: Percentages must add to 100
chunks.body: Since a compound is made up entirely of its elements, all their [[chem-percentage-composition|percentage compositions]] must add up to 100%. This is a handy way to check your working.
chunks.checkText: The percentage compositions of all elements in a compound should add up to...

chunks.heading: Finding a mass from a percentage
chunks.body: To find the mass of one element in a sample, multiply its [[chem-percentage-composition|percentage]] by the total mass, then divide by 100.
chunks.checkText: To find the mass of an element in a sample, you...

checkOptions.text: Multiply its percentage by the total mass, then divide by 100
Divide its percentage by the total mass
Add its percentage to the total mass

chunks.heading: Element names and symbols
chunks.body: Every [[chem-element-basics|element]] has its own chemical symbol, made of one or two letters. The first letter is always a capital, and a second letter, if there is one, is always lower case.
chunks.checkText: In a two-letter chemical symbol, the second letter is always...

checkOptions.text: The same as the first letter

chunks.heading: Metals, non-metals and metalloids
chunks.body: The periodic table sorts elements into three classes: metals, non-metals and metalloids. Most elements are metals.
chunks.checkText: The periodic table divides elements into which three classes?

chunks.heading: What metals are like
chunks.body: [[chem-metals-nonmetals-metalloids|Metals]] are typically shiny, easy to bend into shape, and good conductors of heat and electricity. Most are solid at room temperature.
chunks.checkText: Which property is typical of metals?

chunks.heading: What non-metals are like
chunks.body: Unlike [[chem-metal-properties|metals]], non-metals are usually dull, brittle if solid, and poor conductors of heat and electricity. Many exist as gases at room temperature.
chunks.checkText: Compared to metals, non-metals are generally...

checkOptions.text: Poor conductors of heat and electricity
Shiny and easy to bend into shape

chunks.heading: What metalloids are like
chunks.body: Metalloids sit between [[chem-metal-properties|metals]] and [[chem-nonmetal-properties|non-metals]]. They can look shiny like metals but are brittle like non-metals, and only conduct electricity moderately.
chunks.checkText: Metalloids conduct electricity...

checkOptions.text: Moderately, better than non-metals but worse than metals

chunks.heading: Alloys: metals mixed together
chunks.body: An alloy is a mixture made mostly of a [[chem-metal-properties|metal]] with small amounts of other elements added. Steel, an alloy of iron and carbon, is stronger than pure iron.
chunks.checkText: An alloy is...

checkOptions.text: A mixture of a metal with other elements
A pure element with no other elements added
Always weaker than the pure metal alone

chunks.heading: Physical properties
chunks.body: A physical property, like colour, density or melting point, can be observed or measured without turning the substance into something new. It's the same idea behind a [[chem-physical-change|physical change]].
chunks.checkText: A physical property can be measured...

checkOptions.text: Without changing what the substance is made of
Only by creating a brand new substance
Only by heating the substance until it reacts

chunks.heading: Chemical properties
chunks.body: Unlike a [[chem-physical-property-def|physical property]], a chemical property describes how a substance reacts and turns into something new, like how easily magnesium burns to form magnesium oxide.
chunks.checkText: A chemical property is revealed when a substance...

checkOptions.text: Reacts and turns into a new substance
Is simply measured, like its mass
Is looked at under a microscope
